node.label: Saidiya Hartman
node.description: Scholar of African American literature and cultural history who makes slavery’s afterlives and the conditions of historical narration central problems. Her 2008 essay joins critical fabulation to restraint and the acknowledgment of unrecoverable lives. In her own account of Wayward Lives, ordinary young Black women are social thinkers and experimenters, rather than pathological cases in state records. Respect and criticism coexist in her reading of Du Bois: she values his intellectual achievement while questioning the Philadelphia survey’s class and gender judgments.

The three books remain unread beyond these descriptions and retrospective accounts. Acknowledged narrative failure and limits of speculation are part of the method. The Du Bois critique is her 2020 statement, not an independently read book passage. Existing roster notes and their earlier unread qualifications remain as historical reading records; the new sources state this later scope. proposed_edges.relationship: Critical fabulation confronts the violence of slavery’s archive while requiring narrative restraint and acknowledging the failure to recover the dead (2008).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hartman’s pp.9 and 11–14, read. She distinguishes speculation from verified recovery and refuses closure; no claim that invention supplies lost testimony is accepted. This personal methodological contribution is different from the existing aggregate archive-to-Atlantic and archive-to-Black-history arrows.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wayward Lives (2019) places ordinary young Black women’s experiments in living at the center of historical explanation, while refusing to reproduce state case files’ pathologizing judgments.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The book’s method is read through Hartman’s 2020 first-person interviews and the 2019 institutional account, not a new whole-book reading. This contribution concerns women’s history and its subjects; the generic archive/Atlantic relationships are retained separately.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hartman admires Du Bois’s intellectual achievement but criticizes the Philadelphia survey’s elite and Victorian judgments about Black intimate life (2020 interview).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Explicit first-person answer to Yannise Jean about Du Bois, read. The criticism is dated to the 2020 interview and limited to these class/gender judgments, rather than a wholesale rejection of Du Bois or a passage independently checked in the 2019 book.

verification.note: Interview read in full. Hartman distinguishes nonfiction from novelistic form, state case files from slavery’s scarcer archive, and ordinary Black women’s experiments from elite-centered histories. Her explicit criticism of Du Bois’s class/gender judgments is read in the answer beginning “Du Bois is so important”; it is dated to this 2020 statement, not asserted as a passage independently read in Wayward Lives.
